extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and EPO examiners (practitioners concerned with European patent prosecution)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing when and how the description must be amended to be consistent with amended claims under EPO practice and Article 84 EPC, including examples of inconsistencies, permissible marking/deletion, and case-law tensions. Useful for drafting/amending European patent applications and responding to objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to adapt the description to amended claims (Article 84 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO considers Article 84 EPC to provide a legal basis requiring that inconsistencies between the claims and the description be removed so that the description is consistent with the claims 'not only in some part but throughout'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is justified as ensuring legal certainty for national post-grant proceedings (Article 69 EPC). Expectation is that the requirement to adapt the description to amended claims will persist; applicants should therefore align description and claims across the whole specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'inconsistency' between description and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An inconsistency is something that could throw doubt on the subject-matter for which protection is sought, thus making the claims unclear or unsupported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this test to decide whether a passage in the description must be amended or marked; the focus is on whether the passage could create doubt for the skilled person about what is protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description passages that suggest unclaimed ways to carry out the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of the description that give the skilled person the impression that they disclose ways to carry out the invention, but are not encompassed by the wording of the claims, are considered inconsistent with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such passages should be deleted or appropriately marked as not falling within the scope of the amended claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of an alternative to a claimed feature with broader or different meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: An inconsistency arises when an alternative to a claimed feature is present in the description with a broader or different meaning than the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description must be amended to remove or mark the broader/different alternative so that it does not cast doubt on the claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature in an embodiment demonstrably incompatible with an independent claim
rubrics_metrics.description: If a feature shown in an embodiment is demonstrably incompatible with the wording of an independent claim, that embodiment is inconsistent with the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent embodiments should be deleted or marked; examiners may point to the incompatibility when raising objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describing a mandatory feature as optional in the description
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must be amended to remove terms that refer to a mandatory feature of an independent claim as being optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner alleges this inconsistency, they should provide an example passage in the description showing the mandatory feature described as optional; applicants should amend the text to remove the optional wording or mark it as not relating to the claimed subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible remediation: deletion or marking of inconsistent subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistent subject-matter must be deleted from the description or marked accordingly. Marking is now considered an equally valid option to deletion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marking must be done in a way that clearly indicates which parts are excluded; generic or vague marks are not acceptable (see 'generic disclaimers' rule). Previously marking was only acceptable in limited circumstances, but the 2022 Guidelines treat marking as an equally valid alternative to deletion.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is not an inconsistency: embodiments with extra features still encompassed by independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An embodiment in the description comprising further features not present in the claims but encompassed by the subject-matter of an independent claim is not considered inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not delete/mark embodiments simply because they include additional (narrower) features; they remain consistent if they fall within the claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is not an inconsistency: implicit features or present by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: If an embodiment in the description fails to explicitly mention one or more features of an independent claim, this is not considered inconsistent if the features are implicit or present by reference to another embodiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of explicit repetition of claim features in every embodiment is acceptable when those features are implicitly or contextually present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit of the doubt to the applicant in borderline cases
rubrics_metrics.description: For borderline cases, where there is genuine doubt as to whether an embodiment is consistent with the claims (not just a disagreement between applicant and examiner), the benefit of the doubt will be given to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If genuine uncertainty exists, examiners should not refuse on inconsistency grounds and should give applicants the advantage; applicants can rely on this principle when disputing marginal objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner obligation to provide at least one example before refusing for inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Before refusing an application due to an inconsistency between the description and the claims, examiners must provide at least one example of such an inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an evidentiary requirement: examiners should cite specific passages. If they assert that a mandatory feature is described as optional, they should provide the exact passage illustrating that inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic disclaimers without specific reference are not allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic disclaimers (e.g., statements such as 'embodiments not falling under the scope of the appended claims are to be considered merely as examples suitable for understanding the invention') introduced at the beginning of the description without indicating which parts of the description they specifically refer to are not allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any marking or disclaimer must be specific as to which embodiments or passages are excluded; blanket disclaimers at the front of the description are insufficient to resolve inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple word replacements (e.g., 'embodiment'→'disclosure') are unacceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not acceptable to merely replace words such as 'embodiment' or 'invention' with terms such as 'disclosure' or 'example' to avoid inconsistency, because such wording is not used consistently by the Boards of Appeal and may leave unclear whether the subject-matter is excluded or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More substantive amendments or precise markings are required rather than superficial wording changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-like clauses: requirement to delete or amend claim-like language
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim-like clauses are clauses in the description which, despite not being labelled as a claim, appear as such; claim-like clauses must be deleted or amended to avoid claim-like language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care should be taken when drafting the description to avoid clauses that read like claims. However, there is some case-law nuance: T1444/20 found certain claim-like clauses could not be mistaken for claims and did not affect claim clarity, and the Guidelines may be inconsistent on whether such clauses always must be removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-law divergence: clarity of claims may negate need for description amendments (T1989/18 and T1444/20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Boards (T1989/18, T1444/20) have held that description amendments are unnecessary if the claims are clear in and of themselves; the need to amend the description depends on case facts and whether the description actually casts doubt on the claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants can argue that clear claims stand alone and do not require description amendment, but recent EPO practice (and T1024/18) tends toward requiring removal of inconsistencies; the law is in flux and may be subject to further referral or guidance.
